newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr struggles to regroup after rout.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr struggles to regroup after rout.

text.p: The Australian dollar was in a daze Wednesday after suffering the biggest one-day fall in a decade. Traders said an orderly correction dissolved into rout offshore Tuesday when the market reacted badly to loose talk of lower interest rates and stripped it of almost three cents.
The fall, however, was seen as a heaven sent opportunity by local exporters and funds desperate to take forex cover.
"It was a dream come true to these guys and they bought in serious size," said Michael workman, a currency analyst at CBA. "That makes me think the dollar's heading higher after all."
By 4.30 pm (0530 GMT) the currency was trying to find its feet at US$0.7975/80 having bounced from a deep offshore low of US$0.7855, but was still far below Tuesday's late US$0.8135/40.

On the crosses, it steadied at 90.28/38 yen after plunging as far as 88.78 overnight, but again was a long way short of Tuesday's late 92.95/05. In trade weighted terms it was sharply lower at 59.3 from a previous 60.5 finish.
This was a savage turn in fortunes for the currency which only Monday had been celebrating a six-year high on the U.S. dollar of US$0.8212 and a four-year peak on the yen at 93.80.
The ostensible cause of the setback was one, Bernie Fraser.

Fraser is a former governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia and his word carried great weight with the market until he retired in September. So when he told a current affairs programme there was room for lower rates in Australia, some offshore investors reacted as though he was still in charge.
"Certainly if you look at what happened, it seems to have followed on from his comments," said Steve Shuster, head of forex at Citibank Australia. "But there's more to it than that."
Pressures had been brewing since the dollar launched itself from a US$0.7815 trough a month ago, reaching US$0.8212 in a frenzy of offshore buying last week.
The entire five percent rise came without a meaningful correction leaving the market, and short term momentum investors in particular, dangerously long of dollars.
"What you had was a big snowball reaction," said Shuster. "The move above 82 cents, and then back down below 81, and 80 after that, triggered sell levels for a lot of long positions."
"It's difficult to say it was very overdone because the market was obviously very long and what we'll find now is the dollar will struggle to trade back through 82," he said.
That was much the verdict of chart analysts, who were rather deflated by the rupture of so many important support levels.
"I hate to say it, but this looks like being the mid-point of a year-long consolidation period," said Darren Spain, a currency analyst with Credit Suisse in New York.
"We've had seven months since the former peak in May, and it could be a few more until the uptrend resumes once more."
He looked for a base to form at US$0.7850 with a ceiling around US$0.8070 or, at most, US$0.8150.

The fundamental support of relatively high yields had not changed, however, with the RBA staying silent this morning despite all the hot air about an easing following the monthly meeting of its policy board on Tuesday.
Analysts interpreted the bank's reticence as a sign policy would remain steady until January at the earliest, thus keeping the dollar's yield premium intact for another month.

"At the end of the day, the AUD will grind higher because the Japanese will keep buying it," said Workman at Commonwealth Bank. "Rates there look set to stay at record lows, so yields here will be attractive whether the RBA moves or not."

Figures on Gross Domestic Product for the September quarter were somewhat lost in all the noise, but essentially showed annual growth jogging along at a reasonable 3.8 percent clip with very little in the way of inflationary pressure.
As a footnote the wild swings in the currency reminded old market hands of the 1980's when the dollar was a plaything of international speculators.
Volatility has declined dramatically since then as Australia made progress on solving its worse economic problems, especially inflation, and dealers rather welcomed its return.
"Volatility is always good for traders and especially so at the start of the month when they can clock up a decent profit and sit on it until bonus time," said one.
"In this case, Santa's come early for the forex market."
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
